summary: This document defines OSPF extensions that add information about the node originating a prefix to the prefix advertisement. They do not change core OSPF route computation, but they help with network analysis, troubleshooting and use cases like traffic engineering.

eli5.summary: Each address notice in a router message should say who first posted it. This document adds that name tag, which helps people find problems later.

questions: find which router advertised a prefix
what is the ospf prefix source router id sub-tlv
how to find which router originated an ospf prefix
what is the ospf prefix source router address
subtitle: Two optional OSPF sub-TLVs that say which router originally announced a prefix, even after it crosses areas.

tldr.problem: OSPF cannot always tell which router originated a prefix: the information is lost when an Area Border Router (ABR) propagates inter-area prefixes, and for external prefixes the true originator may be outside the OSPF domain.
tldr.mechanism: Two optional sub-TLVs, Prefix Source OSPF Router-ID and Prefix Source Router Address, are added to prefix advertisements to carry the originating router's Router ID and a reachable address.
tldr.outcome: The extensions do not change OSPF route computation, but they help with network analysis, troubleshooting and traffic engineering, for example on a controller fed through BGP-LS.

today: RFC 9084 is a Proposed Standard published in August 2021. It has not been obsoleted or updated, so it remains the definition of the OSPF prefix originator sub-TLVs.

sections.title: Why the Originator Gets Lost
sections.content:
OSPFv2 advertises prefix attributes in the Extended Prefix Opaque LSA (RFC 7684), and OSPFv3 uses the Extended Prefix LSA types (RFC 8362). Finding the router that originated a prefix is not always possible.

  • For intra-area prefixes, the originator is the Advertising Router of the area-scoped LSA.
  • For inter-area prefixes, the Advertising Router is the ABR itself, so the original originator is lost as the prefix crosses areas.
  • For AS external prefixes, the ASBR is identified, but the real originator may be a remote router outside the OSPF domain. The same happens when an ABR translates NSSA LSAs to AS-external LSAs.

The OSPF Router ID is a 32-bit number that is unique in the domain, but it is not necessarily a reachable address. The IPv4 and IPv6 Router Address of RFC 3630 and RFC 5329 provides an address to reach the router.
sections.eli5: When a note is passed along through many hands, the name of the first writer gets rubbed off. Sometimes you need to know who wrote it.

sections.title: What the Originator Information Is For
sections.content:
The primary use case is identifying the originator of a prefix. It also lets you associate all prefixes from one router, even when they are advertised outside the area where they originated, and spot when the same prefix is originated by multiple routers across areas.

The extensions do not change core OSPF route computation. They provide information for topology analysis and traffic engineering, especially on a controller when the information is advertised as a prefix attribute through BGP-LS (RFC 7752, RFC 9085).
sections.eli5: Knowing who first posted a notice helps a detective follow the trail when something goes wrong.

sections.title: The Two Sub-TLVs
sections.content:
Both sub-TLVs are optional. For OSPFv2 they sit inside the Extended Prefix TLV. For OSPFv3 they sit inside the Intra-Area-Prefix, Inter-Area-Prefix and External-Prefix TLVs, for either an IPv4 or an IPv6 prefix advertisement.

The Prefix Source OSPF Router-ID sub-TLV has Type 4 for OSPFv2 and 27 for OSPFv3, Length 4, and carries the OSPF Router ID of the router that originated the prefix in the OSPF domain.

The Prefix Source Router Address sub-TLV has Type 5 for OSPFv2 and 28 for OSPFv3, and Length 4 or 16. It carries a reachable IPv4 or IPv6 address of the originating router, semantically equal to what may be advertised in the OSPFv2 Router Address TLV or OSPFv3 Router IPv6 Address TLV.

The parent TLV MAY include more than one of each, one for each Equal-Cost Multipath (ECMP) node that originated the prefix.
sections.eli5: There are two name tags. One has the router's ID number. The other has an address where you can actually reach it.

sections.title: Validation Rules
sections.content:
For intra-area prefixes, a Prefix Source OSPF Router-ID sub-TLV MUST be considered invalid and ignored if its Router ID differs from the Advertising Router field of the containing LSA. The RFC says similar validation cannot be reliably done for inter-area and external prefixes.

A Router-ID sub-TLV with the Router ID set to 0 MUST be considered invalid and ignored. A Router Address sub-TLV whose length is not consistent with the prefix's address family MUST also be ignored. In both cases the reception SHOULD be logged as an error, subject to rate limiting.
sections.eli5: If a name tag looks wrong, such as a blank name, the router ignores it and quietly writes a note in its log.

sections.title: Elements of Procedure
sections.content:
The Router ID field is set to the OSPF Router ID of the originating node. If that node advertises an OSPFv2 Router Address TLV or OSPFv3 Router IPv6 Address TLV, the same address MUST be used in the Router Address sub-TLV. Otherwise an implementation can pick a unique, reachable local address, for example one advertised with the N-Flag or N-bit set.

When an ABR passes an inter-area prefix from the backbone area into a non-backbone area, the only way to learn the originator is from the sub-TLVs in the advertisement that another ABR placed in the backbone. The ABR does its prefix calculation to find the nodes contributing ECMP paths and MUST only use originator information from that set. It MUST NOT include the sub-TLVs if it cannot determine the information for those nodes.

For prefixes redistributed from another routing domain, the mechanism is outside the scope of the RFC. Implementations may let the operator choose whether the Router Address is the ASBR or the actual node outside the OSPF domain. An NSSA ABR translating NSSA prefixes to AS external prefixes follows the same procedure as for inter-area prefixes.
sections.eli5: A router in the middle copies the name tag only if it is sure whose tag it is. If it is not sure, it leaves the tag off instead of guessing.

sections.title: Operational Considerations
sections.content:
The extra sub-TLVs increase the size of the OSPF Link-State Database, so the impact should be considered. Depending on design, only a subset of prefixes might carry originator information.

Propagating this information across area or domain boundaries exposes details that the base OSPF protocol would normally hide or abstract. Depending on design, ABRs or ASBRs may limit the propagation to a subset of prefixes. The information may also aid debugging of prefix reachability problems.
sections.eli5: Name tags make the notice board bigger and show things that used to be private, so you may only tag the notices that matter.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Because the document extends the OSPFv2 Extended Prefix LSA and the OSPFv3 E-Intra-Area-Prefix-LSA, E-Inter-Area-Prefix-LSA, E-AS-External-LSA and E-NSSA-LSA, the security considerations of RFC 7684 and RFC 8362 apply. The new sub-TLVs are optional and do not affect OSPF route computation, so they do not affect the security of OSPF operations.

A rogue node that can inject prefix advertisements could use these extensions to advertise bogus prefix source information.
sections.eli5: A sneaky router could write a fake name on a tag, but the tags do not decide where traffic goes.

fields.name: OSPF Router ID
fields.desc: Router ID of the router that originated the prefix advertisement.
